cse-2002-b-51-a.approach: A binary relation on $A$ is any subset of $A\times A$, so count the subsets of a set of $n^2$ ordered pairs.

steps.title: Size of A × A
steps.body: A binary relation on $A$ is a subset of $A\times A$, and $|A\times A| = n\cdot n = n^2$.

steps.title: Count subsets
steps.body:
Each of the $n^2$ ordered pairs is either in the relation or not: $2$ choices per pair, so
$$N_r = \underbrace{2\cdot 2\cdots 2}_{n^2} = 2^{n^2}.$$

pitfalls: Writing $2^{2n}$ or $2^n$ — the relation chooses among $n^2$ pairs, not $n$ or $2n$ elements.
cse-2002-b-51-a.verification: $n=1$: $A\times A$ has one pair, relations are $\emptyset$ and $\{(1,1)\}$, i.e. $2 = 2^{1}$. $n=2$: $2^4 = 16$ subsets of the 4 pairs.

cse-2002-b-51-b.approach: A function $A\to A$ picks exactly one image for each of the $n$ elements; apply the product rule.

steps.title: Choices per element
steps.body: Each element $x\in A$ must be mapped to exactly one of the $n$ elements of $A$: $n$ choices.

steps.title: Product rule
steps.body:
The $n$ choices are independent, so
$$N_f = \underbrace{n\cdot n\cdots n}_{n} = n^n.$$

pitfalls: Counting only bijections ($n!$) — functions need not be one-one or onto.

cse-2002-b-51-c.approach: Every function is itself a relation (its graph), and for $n\ge1$ there are relations that are not functions, so $N_r > N_f$; algebraically $2^{n^2} = (2^n)^n > n^n$.

steps.title: Compare the formulas
steps.body: $N_r = 2^{n^2} = (2^n)^n$ and $N_f = n^n$. Since $2^n > n$ for every $n\ge 1$, raising both positive sides to the power $n$ gives $(2^n)^n > n^n$.

steps.title: Set-inclusion view
steps.body: Each function $f$ is the relation $\{(x, f(x))\}$, so functions are a subset of relations; the empty relation is not a function, so the inclusion is strict and $N_r > N_f$.

cse-2002-b-52-a.approach: Check the diagonal for irreflexivity, then add the fewest pairs needed for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity.

steps.title: Irreflexive?
steps.body: A relation is irreflexive when no $(x,x)$ belongs to it. $S$ contains only $\langle1,2\rangle$ and $\langle2,1\rangle$, so none of $\langle1,1\rangle,\langle2,2\rangle,\langle3,3\rangle$ is present: **$S$ is irreflexive**.

steps.title: Reflexive closure
steps.body: An equivalence relation on $A=\{1,2,3\}$ must contain every $\langle x,x\rangle$, so add $\langle1,1\rangle,\langle2,2\rangle,\langle3,3\rangle$ (3 pairs — unavoidable).

steps.title: Symmetry and transitivity
steps.body: Symmetric: $\langle1,2\rangle$ and $\langle2,1\rangle$ both present. Transitive: $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle2,1\rangle$ give $\langle1,1\rangle$ and $\langle2,1\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle$ give $\langle2,2\rangle$, both already added. Nothing more is needed; the classes are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3\}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting $\langle3,3\rangle$ — reflexivity is required for every element of $A$, even one not mentioned in $S$.
Confusing irreflexive with "not reflexive".
cse-2002-b-52-a.verification: The result is the partition $\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\}$, which needs exactly $2^2+1^2 = 5$ pairs; $S$ had 2, so 3 is the minimum to add.

cse-2002-b-52-b.approach: List the four subsets, keep only the covering relations of $\subseteq$ (no reflexive or transitive edges), and draw larger sets higher.

steps.title: Elements
steps.body: $\mathcal{P}(S) = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\}$.

steps.title: Covering pairs
steps.body: $\emptyset \subset \{a\}$, $\emptyset \subset \{b\}$, $\{a\} \subset \{a,b\}$, $\{b\} \subset \{a,b\}$ are covers (nothing lies strictly between). $\emptyset \subset \{a,b\}$ follows by transitivity, so it is **not** drawn; $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ are incomparable.

steps.title: Diagram
steps.body: The result is a diamond: $\emptyset$ at the bottom (least element), $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ in the middle, $\{a,b\}$ at the top (greatest element). Meet $=\cap$, join $=\cup$.

answer.value: A diamond: $\emptyset$ at the bottom, $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ in the middle, $\{a,b\}$ at the top, with edges $\emptyset$–$\{a\}$, $\emptyset$–$\{b\}$, $\{a\}$–$\{a,b\}$, $\{b\}$–$\{a,b\}$

pitfalls: Drawing the edge $\emptyset$–$\{a,b\}$ (implied by transitivity) or self-loops.
cse-2002-b-52-b.verification: 4 elements and 4 cover edges; it is the Boolean lattice $B_2$, isomorphic to $\{0,1\}^2$.

cse-2002-b-53-a.approach: The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries.

steps.title: Triangular structure
steps.body: All entries below the main diagonal are $0$, so $A-\lambda I$ is also upper triangular and its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

steps.title: Characteristic polynomial
steps.body:
$$\det(A-\lambda I) = (1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)(-2-\lambda)(-1-\lambda) = 0$$
so $\lambda = 1, 2, -2, -1$.

pitfalls: Getting distracted by the large off-diagonal entries (34, 49, 43, 94, 104) — they do not affect the eigenvalues.

cse-2002-b-53-b.approach: Simplify each formula with idempotence/absorption/De Morgan, falling back on a single assignment to show "neither".

steps.title: (i) A ↔ (A ∨ A)
steps.body: Idempotence: $A\vee A \equiv A$, so the formula is $A\leftrightarrow A$, true for both values of $A$: **tautology**.

steps.title: (ii) (A ∨ B) → B
steps.body:
$A=1,B=0$: $(1\vee0)\rightarrow0 = 1\rightarrow0 = 0$ (false).
$A=0,B=1$: $1\rightarrow1 = 1$ (true).
It is sometimes true and sometimes false: **neither**. (It simplifies to $\neg A\vee B$, i.e. $A\rightarrow B$.)

steps.title: (iii) A ∧ ¬(A ∨ B)
steps.body:
De Morgan: $
eg(A\vee B) \equiv 
eg A\wedge
eg B$, so the formula is $A\wedge
eg A\wedge
eg B \equiv 0\wedge
eg B \equiv 0$: **contradiction**.

cse-2002-b-54.approach: Preorder visits the root first, so C is the root and B, A (in that order) must be the preorder of C’s subtrees; enumerate where B and A can sit.

steps.title: Root is C
steps.body: Preorder is root, left, right, so the first symbol $C$ is the root. The remaining sequence $B, A$ is the preorder of $C$’s left subtree followed by its right subtree.

steps.title: Case 1: B, A both in the left subtree
steps.body: The left subtree has preorder $B,A$, so $B$ is its root and $A$ is a child of $B$ — left or right. This gives 2 trees. Tree 1: $A$ is the left child of $B$.

steps.title: Case 1, second tree
steps.body: Tree 2: $A$ is the right child of $B$, $B$ the left child of $C$. Preorder: $C, B, A$.

steps.title: Case 2: B, A both in the right subtree
steps.body: Symmetrically, $B$ is the right child of $C$ and $A$ is the left (tree 3) or right (tree 4) child of $B$.

steps.title: Case 2, second tree
steps.body: Tree 4: the right-going chain $C \to B \to A$. Preorder: $C, B, A$.

steps.title: Case 3: split between subtrees
steps.body: Left subtree $=\{B\}$, right subtree $=\{A\}$ (the order $B$ before $A$ forces $B$ to the left). Tree 5. The split $A$ left, $B$ right would give $C,A,B$, so it is excluded. Total $2+2+1 = 5$ trees.

answer.value: 5 binary trees: C with left child B (A left or right of B); C with right child B (A left or right of B); C with left child B and right child A

cse-2002-b-54.shortcut: For a fixed preorder of $n$ distinct labels, the number of binary trees equals the number of shapes, the Catalan number $C_n$; $C_3 = \frac{1}{4}\binom{6}{3} = 5$.
pitfalls: Missing the trees where $A$ is a left child of $B$ — preorder does not distinguish left from right when the other side is empty.
cse-2002-b-54.verification: Catalan number $C_3 = 5$ matches the enumeration, and each tree’s preorder was checked to be $C, B, A$.

cse-2002-b-55-a.approach: Add the consensus term $xz'$ so the sum of products factors as $(x+y)(y'+z')$; then De Morgan turns $y'+z'$ into a single complement $(yz)'$.

steps.title: Add the consensus term
steps.body:
In $xy' + yz'$ the variable $y$ appears complemented in one term and uncomplemented in the other, so the consensus term is $x\cdot z'$:
$$f = xy' + yz' + xz'.$$

steps.title: Factor
steps.body: Expand $(x+y)(y'+z') = xy' + xz' + yy' + yz' = xy' + xz' + 0 + yz'$, which equals $f$. Hence $f = (x+y)(y'+z')$.

steps.title: One complement
steps.body:
De Morgan: $y'+z' = (yz)'$, so
$$f = (x+y)\cdot(yz)'.$$
Circuit: OR gate on $x,y$; AND gate on $y,z$ followed by the single NOT gate; a final AND gate combines the two.

scene.caption: f = (x + y)·(yz)′ with one NOT gate

pitfalls: Writing $f = x(yz)' + \dots$ with two complements, or forgetting that the factorisation only works after adding the consensus term.
cse-2002-b-55-a.verification: Truth table over $xyz = 000\ldots111$: $f = 0,0,1,0,1,1,1,0$ for both $xy'+yz'$ and $(x+y)(yz)'$.

cse-2002-b-55-b.approach: AND–OR becomes NAND–NAND, but the circuit has two cascaded OR levels; insert one NAND used as an inverter so the second OR level is again a NAND fed by complemented inputs.

steps.title: First AND–OR level
steps.body:
Label the inputs $a,b$; $c,d$; $e,f$. By bubble pushing, AND gates feeding an OR gate become NAND gates feeding a NAND gate:
$N_1 = \overline{ab}$, $N_2 = \overline{cd}$, $N_3 = \text{NAND}(N_1,N_2)$, which equals the first OR output ($ab + cd$).

steps.title: Second OR level
steps.body: The second OR needs complemented inputs to become a NAND. The third AND gives $N_5 = \overline{ef}$ (already complemented). The first OR output must be inverted: $N_4 = \text{NAND}(N_3,N_3)$ (a NAND with its inputs tied acts as NOT).

steps.title: Output gate
steps.body: $N_6 = \text{NAND}(N_4, N_5)$ — this replaces the second OR gate. Gate count: $N_1\ldots N_6 = 6$ two-input NAND gates.

scene.caption: Six 2-input NAND gates (N4 is a NAND used as an inverter)

pitfalls: Feeding $N_3$ straight into the last NAND — $N_3$ is uncomplemented, so the output would be wrong without the inverter $N_4$.
cse-2002-b-55-b.verification: Bubble check: $N_3 = \overline{\overline{ab}\cdot\overline{cd}} = ab+cd$; $N_6 = \overline{\overline{N_3}\cdot\overline{ef}} = N_3 + ef = ab + cd + ef$, the original circuit.

cse-2002-b-56-a.approach: Each falling edge shifts the data one stage down: R0 takes the new inputs, R1 the first-stage result of R0, R2 the second-stage result of R1. So after clock $k$, R2 holds pair $k-2$ and $Z$ (from the last full adder) is $A_{k-2}+B_{k-2}$.

steps.title: Stage timing
steps.body: Stage 1 (FA under R0) adds $a_0+b_0$ into R1; stage 2 adds $a_1+b_1+c_1$ into R2; stage 3 (FA under R2) is combinational and drives $z_3z_2$, with $z_1=s_1$, $z_0=s_0$ taken from R2. Hence $Z$ after clock $k$ is the sum of the pair loaded at clock $k-2$.

steps.title: Clocks 1–2: pipeline filling
steps.body: After clocks 1 and 2, R2 still holds its initial zeros, so $Z = 0+0 = 0000$ both times.

steps.title: Clocks 7–8
steps.body: R2 now holds pairs 5 and 6, both $000+000$, so $Z = 0000$ after clocks 7 and 8.

animation.caption: Contents after each falling edge (pair # loaded at that clock)

pitfalls: Producing $1011$ already after clock 1 — the result needs two more edges to reach R2.
Treating stage 3 as registered — $Z$ comes from a combinational full adder after R2.

cse-2002-b-56-b.approach: Read the data path: one full adder per bit position, carries passed down through registers, unused bits delayed alongside — a ripple-carry adder cut into stages by registers.

steps.title: Per-stage work
steps.body: Stage 1 adds bit 0 ($a_0+b_0+0$), stage 2 adds bit 1 with the carry from stage 1, stage 3 adds bit 2 with the carry from stage 2 and outputs the final carry $z_3$. Each carry travels to the next stage through a register.

steps.title: Why the extra register bits
steps.body: The higher bits ($a_2,b_2,a_1,b_1$) and the already computed sum bits ($s_0$, later $s_1$) are copied down unchanged so they stay aligned with their own operation. A new addition can start every clock; each result appears 2 clocks after its inputs are loaded (Z = 1011 after clock 3 for the pair loaded at clock 1).

answer.value: A 3-stage pipelined 3-bit (ripple-carry) binary adder: $Z = A + B$ (4-bit result), one addition per clock with a latency of 2 clocks

pitfalls: Calling it a serial adder — all three bit-additions of different operand pairs are in progress simultaneously.
cse-2002-b-56-b.verification: Part (a) gives $Z = A+B$ for every input pair, two clocks after loading.

cse-2002-b-57-a.approach: Write $7.5$ as a base-16 fraction with a non-zero leading hex digit, bias the exponent by 64, then pack sign | fraction | exponent and read the 32 bits in hex.

steps.title: Normalise in base 16
steps.body: $7.5 = 7.8_{16} = 0.78_{16}\times16^1$. The leading hex digit $7 \ne 0$, so it is normalised. Fraction bits: $0111\,1000$ followed by 16 zeros, i.e. $780000_{16}$.

steps.title: Sign and exponent
steps.body: Negative, so sign $=1$. Exponent $=1+64 = 65 = 1000001_2 = 41_{16}$ (7 bits).

pitfalls: Normalising in base 2 ($0.1111\times2^3$) — the base is 16, so only the leading hex digit must be non-zero.
Forgetting that the 4-bit nibbles straddle the field boundaries when converting the whole word to hex.

cse-2002-b-57-b.approach: Largest value = largest fraction × $16^{\text{largest exponent}}$; convert to a power of 10 with logarithms.

steps.title: Extreme fields
steps.body: Largest fraction $=0.\text{FFFFFF}_{16} = 1-16^{-6} = 1-2^{-24}\approx1$. Largest exponent field $=127$, so the exponent is $127-64 = 63$.

steps.title: Convert
steps.body: Max $\approx16^{63} = 2^{252}$. $\log_{10}2^{252} = 252\times0.30103 = 75.86$, so the value is $\approx 10^{75.86}\approx 7.2\times10^{75}$, nearest power of ten $10^{76}$.

pitfalls: Using exponent $+64$ (field 127 means $127-64=63$).
cse-2002-b-57-b.verification: $10^{75.86}$ lies between $10^{75.5}$ and $10^{76}$, so $10^{76}$ is the nearest power of 10.

cse-2002-b-58-a.approach: Map each element to its cache line: line $=\lfloor\text{address}/16\rfloor \bmod 512$. Two elements conflict only if they map to the same line but lie in different memory blocks.

steps.title: Cache geometry
steps.body: Lines $= 8\,\text{KB}/16\,\text{B} = 8192/16 = 512$. Element $A[i]$ is at byte address $4i$, in memory block $\lfloor4i/16\rfloor = \lfloor i/4\rfloor$ and cache line $\lfloor i/4\rfloor \bmod 512$.

steps.title: Who maps to line 0?
steps.body: $A[0]$ is in block 0, line 0. Another block maps to line 0 only if its block number is a multiple of 512, i.e. byte address $\ge 512\times16 = 8192$, i.e. $i \ge 2048$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The array is $2048\times4 = 8192$ bytes — exactly the cache size, so indices $0..2047$ occupy blocks $0..511$, each on its own line. **No element conflicts with $A[0]$.** $A[1], A[2], A[3]$ share line 0 with $A[0]$ but are in the same block, so they are brought in together rather than evicting it.

answer.value: None — the 8 KB array fits exactly in the 8 KB cache (blocks 0–511 map to distinct lines); $A[1..3]$ share $A[0]$’s block, so they do not conflict
answer.keyNote: The stored key ("Base address + 4 * 2048 = 8192 bytes = 2 pages of 4 KB each") does not name any conflicting element and talks about pages, which are irrelevant to cache mapping. The first element that would map to line 0 from a different block is at byte 8192, i.e. $A[2048]$, outside the array; so no element of the array conflicts with $A[0]$.

pitfalls: Calling $A[1..3]$ conflicts — same block means same tag, so they hit together.
Mixing pages (virtual memory) with cache lines.
cse-2002-b-58-a.verification: Total blocks in the array $= 8192/16 = 512 =$ number of cache lines, so the block-to-line map $b\mapsto b \bmod 512$ is one-to-one on the array.

cse-2002-b-58-b.approach: In a reverse sweep each 16-byte block (4 floats) misses once on its first-touched element; since the whole array fits in the cache without conflicts, nothing is evicted.

steps.title: Blocks touched
steps.body: Elements per block $=16/4 = 4$. Blocks in the array $= 2048/4 = 512$.

steps.title: Misses per block
steps.body: Going from $A[2047]$ down, the first access to a block (e.g. $A[2047]$ for block 511) misses and loads $A[2044..2047]$; the next 3 accesses hit. No eviction can occur because the 512 blocks map to 512 distinct lines (part a).

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Misses $= 512\text{ blocks}\times1 = 512$ (all compulsory); hits $= 2048-512 = 1536$.

answer.value: 512 misses (one compulsory miss per 16-byte block; no conflict misses)

pitfalls: Answering 2048 — that ignores that a 16-byte line brings in 4 elements at once.
cse-2002-b-58-b.verification: Direction does not matter for compulsory misses: forward order also gives $2048/4 = 512$.

cse-2002-b-59.approach: Read the parameters as move($n$, source, auxiliary, destination): the printf moves disk $n$ from A to C, so first park $n-1$ disks on B (using C), then bring them from B to C (using A).

steps.title: Base condition
steps.body: The body must run only while disks remain: `if (n > 0)`. For $n=0$ nothing is printed.

steps.title: First recursive call
steps.body: Before disk $n$ can go from A to C, the top $n-1$ disks must move from A to B using C as the spare: `move(n-1, A, C, B)` (source A, auxiliary C, destination B).

steps.title: Second recursive call

answer.value: `if (n > 0)`, `move(n-1, A, C, B)`, `move(n-1, B, A, C)`

pitfalls: Swapping the roles in the first call (`move(n-1, A, B, C)`) — that would put the $n-1$ disks on C, blocking disk $n$.
cse-2002-b-59.verification: $n=2$: prints "disk 1 A→B", "disk 2 A→C", "disk 1 B→C" — a valid 3-move solution ($2^2-1$).

cse-2002-b-60-a.approach: With unit edge weights, a direct edge gives path length 1 and a missing edge must start as "no path known", i.e. $\infty$, so that min() ignores it.

steps.title: No edge
steps.body: If $A[i,j]=0$ there is no direct path, so $P[i,j]$ must be $\infty$ (a value larger than any real path length, e.g. $n$ or more); using $0$ would make min() pick a non-existent path.

steps.title: Edge
steps.body: If $A[i,j]=1$ the direct edge is a path of length 1, so $P[i,j] = 1$ (equivalently $A[i,j]$).

pitfalls: Initialising missing edges to 0.
cse-2002-b-60-a.verification: After the algorithm, $P[i,j]$ is the minimum number of edges on an $i\to j$ path, and stays $\infty$ exactly when $j$ is unreachable from $i$.

cse-2002-b-60-b.approach: The outermost loop variable $i$ must be the intermediate vertex (Floyd–Warshall’s phase), so relax every pair $(j,k)$ through $i$.

steps.title: Identify the intermediate vertex
steps.body: Floyd–Warshall’s invariant: after phase $i$, $P[j,k]$ is the shortest $j\to k$ path using only intermediates from $\{1,\dots,i\}$. The phase variable must be the **outermost** loop, which here is $i$.

steps.title: Relaxation line
steps.body:
Inside, update every pair through vertex $i$:
$$P[j,k] = \min\{P[j,k],\ P[j,i] + P[i,k]\}$$

pitfalls: Writing $P[i,j] = \min\{P[i,j], P[i,k]+P[k,j]\}$ — with $k$ innermost this is not Floyd–Warshall and gives wrong results.

cse-2002-b-60-c.approach: Three nested loops of $n$ iterations each with constant work inside.

steps.title: Count iterations
steps.body: Loops over $i$, $j$, $k$ each run $n$ times, so the min() line runs $n\cdot n\cdot n = n^3$ times; each execution is $O(1)$.

steps.title: Initialisation
steps.body: The initialisation is $n^2$ steps, dominated by $n^3$. Total: $O(n^3)$.

cse-2002-b-61-a.approach: An ordered sum $n = x_1 + x_2$ is fixed once $x_1$ is chosen from $1..n-1$.

steps.title: Choose the first part
steps.body: $x_1 \ge 1$ and $x_2 = n - x_1 \ge 1 \Rightarrow 1 \le x_1 \le n-1$: $n-1$ choices, each giving a different ordered pair.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $n=3$: $x_1\in\{1,2\}$ gives $1+2, 2+1$ — 2 ways, matching the example.

pitfalls: Counting unordered sums ($\lfloor n/2\rfloor$) — the example counts $1+2$ and $2+1$ separately.

cse-2002-b-61-b.approach: Stars and bars: place 2 dividers in the $n-1$ gaps between $n$ ones.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Write $n$ as $1+1+\dots+1$; there are $n-1$ gaps between the ones. Choosing 2 distinct gaps for dividers splits them into 3 positive ordered parts, and every composition arises exactly once.

cse-2002-b-61-c.approach: Generalise stars and bars: $k$ positive parts need $k-1$ dividers in the $n-1$ gaps.

steps.title: Dividers
steps.body: Among the $n-1$ gaps between $n$ ones, choose $k-1$ for dividers; this yields $k$ non-empty ordered groups, i.e. $x_1+\dots+x_k = n$ with each $x_i\ge1$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body:
$$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$$
Checks: $k=2$ gives $n-1$ (part a); $k=3$ gives $\binom{n-1}{2}$ (part b).

pitfalls: Using $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$, which counts non-negative parts.
cse-2002-b-61-c.verification: Substituting $y_i = x_i-1\ge0$: $\sum y_i = n-k$, with $\binom{(n-k)+k-1}{k-1} = \binom{n-1}{k-1}$ solutions.

cse-2002-b-62-a.approach: Build $M$ (from $\langle M',x\rangle$) so its input is irrelevant: it discards $w$ and runs $M'$ on the hard-wired $x$.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: $M$ has $M'$ and $x$ built into its states. On input $w$, it first **erases $w$, writes $x$ on the tape and simulates $M'$ on $x$**.

steps.title: Why ignore w
steps.body: The target language demands "halts and outputs 1 **irrespective of the input**"; making $M$’s behaviour independent of $w$ turns that "for all inputs" condition into a single question: does $M'$ halt on $x$?

answer.value: Ignore (erase) $w$, write $x$ on the tape and simulate $M'$ on $x$

cse-2002-b-62-a.verification: This is the standard reduction from HALT; the map $\langle M',x\rangle\mapsto M$ is computable since it only writes out a fixed program around $M'$ and $x$.

cse-2002-b-62-b.approach: If the simulation finishes, output 1 and halt; if it never finishes, $M$ never halts.

steps.title: Second step
steps.body: If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts (whatever $M'$ outputs), $M$ **writes 1 on its tape and halts**. If $M'$ runs forever on $x$, the simulation never ends and $M$ never halts.

steps.title: Resulting property
steps.body: So $M$ halts with output 1 on every $w$ $\iff$ $M'$ halts on $x$. A decider for the target language would decide HALT, which is impossible — hence the language is undecidable.

answer.value: If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts, $M$ outputs 1 and halts (otherwise it runs forever)

pitfalls: Outputting $M'$’s own result — it must be 1 regardless of what $M'$ outputs.
cse-2002-b-62-b.verification: Both directions: $M'$ halts on $x$ ⇒ $M$ outputs 1 on all $w$; $M'$ loops on $x$ ⇒ $M$ halts on no $w$.
